html:
A league of city-states in Etruria, central Italy, roughly modern Tuscany, western Umbria and northern Lazio. The Etruscans flourished from about 900 BCE until Rome absorbed them in the 3rd century BCE. Before Rome's rise, they were the leading power of Italy.

They grew out of the Villanovan culture of the early Iron Age. Rich in iron and copper, they traded with the Greeks and with Phoenicians and Carthage, and grew wealthy. At their height they spread north into the Po Valley and south into Campania.

What they were like:

  • Twelve leading cities, such as Veii, Tarquinia, Caere and Volsinii, formed a loose league that met at a shared shrine, but they rarely acted as one.
  • They spoke a language unlike Latin or Greek and not Indo-European. They wrote it in an alphabet borrowed from the Greeks, which we can read, but we understand only part of the language.
  • Their painted tombs show banquets, music, dancing and games, with women dining alongside men, which shocked the Greeks.
  • Their priests read the will of the gods in the livers of sacrificed animals and in lightning.

Etruscans shaped early Rome. Its last kings, the Tarquins, were Etruscan, and Rome took from them the fasces, much of its religion and ways of building. Ancient writers also credited them with the toga and gladiator games. After Rome expelled its last king in 509 BCE, the two fought for centuries. Rome took Veii in 396 BCE, and by 264 BCE, with the fall of Volsinii, the Etruscan cities were all under Roman rule. Their people became Roman citizens after 90 BCE, and the language died out.
